titre: The gas Cavendish had already spotted, without understanding it
accroche: A 0.5% difference in the density of nitrogen from air led, in 1894, to the discovery of a gas that had always been breathed but never seen.
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1892, the British physicist Lord Rayleigh weighs nitrogen obtained in two different ways: by removing the oxygen, water vapor, and carbon dioxide from air, and by chemically decomposing nitrogen compounds such as ammonia. The two samples should weigh the same. They do not: the nitrogen taken from air is consistently about 0.5% heavier, however precise he makes his balances.

## A gap too small to be an error

Rayleigh publishes the anomaly rather than filing it away as a measurement artifact, and publicly asks whether anyone has an explanation. The chemist William Ramsay answers him, and the two men team up to hunt it down. The simplest hypothesis: the nitrogen in air contains a gas heavier than itself, in an amount too small to have ever been isolated.

To test it, Ramsay removes from air, one by one, every gas that the chemistry of the day knows how to recognize: oxygen, burned over hot copper, then the nitrogen itself, absorbed by reacting it with glowing-hot magnesium. A residue remains, about one hundredth of the starting volume, which refuses to react with anything presented to it. Its light spectrum matches no known element. On January 31, 1895, Rayleigh and Ramsay present their results to the Royal Society of London under the title “Argon, a New Constituent of the Atmosphere” and propose that name, from the Greek *argos*, inactive.

An older observation now takes on its full meaning. In 1785, the chemist Henry Cavendish had already burned atmospheric nitrogen with excess oxygen, until a residue of about one hundredth persisted and would not react further. He had recorded the fact without being able to explain it. For more than a century, that residue remained a line of incomprehension in a laboratory notebook, for lack of an instrument able to say what chemistry could not make react.

## The first of a hidden family

The discovery immediately changes how people search. If an inert gas escaped a century of chemistry, others may have done the same. As early as February 1895, Ramsay heats a sample of cleveite, a uranium ore, and finds in it a gas whose spectrum matches a line spotted in sunlight twenty-seven years earlier, in 1868, and never seen on Earth since: helium. Three years later, Ramsay and Morris Travers isolate neon, krypton, and xenon in the residues of liquefied air.

Argon today makes up 0.93% of the atmosphere, roughly one breath of air in a hundred. It had been there in every breath forever, alongside the nitrogen and oxygen that had been named since the 18th century. What made it invisible was not its scarcity but the absence of any chemical reaction by which to detect it, until a 0.5% discrepancy on a balance forced people to look for it another way.

repere.texte: Rayleigh and Ramsay announce the discovery of argon before the Royal Society of London on January 31, 1895: a gas that makes up 0.93% of Earth's atmosphere and that had never been identified because it reacts with nothing.
repere.source: Rayleigh & Ramsay, “Argon, a New Constituent of the Atmosphere,” Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society A, 186, 1895

carte.punch: A 0.5% density gap flushed out a gas that had always been breathed.
carte.idee: In 1892, Rayleigh finds that nitrogen taken from air weighs about 0.5% more than nitrogen derived from chemical compounds. The investigation flushes out argon, an inert gas that Cavendish had already spotted in 1785 without being able to explain it. It makes up 0.93% of air today.
carte.source_courte: Rayleigh & Ramsay, Phil. Trans. R. Soc. A, 1895

quiz.question: Why did the residue Cavendish isolated in 1785 remain misunderstood for more than a century?
choix: Because the chemistry of the time identified a gas only by making it react, and this one reacted with nothing
Because Cavendish never published the observation, keeping it to his private notebooks
Because the residue was only an undetectable trace, less than a thousandth of the air
Because no balance of the era could weigh so rare a gas
quiz.explication: Argon's chemical inertness is precisely what made it undetectable: with no reaction, 18th-century chemistry had no purchase on it. Cavendish did publish his measurement, and the residue already amounted to nearly one hundredth of the air, a quantity his balance could easily weigh.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How does Lord Rayleigh obtain the two nitrogen samples whose difference in weight sets off the investigation?
choix: The first by liquefying air, the second by heating it to a high temperature
The first in a London laboratory, the second in a Paris laboratory
The first before the discovery of helium, the second after, to check the result
The first by removing oxygen from air, the second by decomposing nitrogen compounds
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Rayleigh compares nitrogen obtained by removing oxygen, water vapor, and carbon dioxide from air with nitrogen drawn chemically from compounds such as ammonia.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does Ramsay find when he heats a sample of cleveite in February 1895?
choix: A second sample of argon, confirming the January 1895 discovery
A gas whose spectrum matches a line spotted in the Sun in 1868: helium
A radioactive compound previously unknown to chemistry
A trace of oxygen trapped in the ore since its formation
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The spectrum of the gas found in cleveite matches a line observed in sunlight in 1868 and never seen on Earth since: it is helium.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What do Ramsay and Morris Travers discover three years after argon, in the residues of liquefied air?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text states that Ramsay and Morris Travers, three years after argon, isolate neon, krypton, and xenon in the residues of liquefied air.
